title: Clean firm power’s next test | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Wood Mackenzie podcast argues AI/data-center demand has revived nuclear and geothermal as clean firm power, but the real test is repeatable, affordable delivery: nuclear uprates/restarts come before 2030s SMRs and hinge on NRC progress, while enhanced geothermal must prove economic reservoirs, with 2028–2030 PPAs as the first delivery test.

insights.claim: Rising electricity demand from AI and data centers has revived interest in nuclear and geothermal as clean firm power, but demand, corporate partnerships and policy support do not by themselves deliver affordable electricity on time.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Discount announcements and PPAs; value clean-firm names on delivered, on-time, affordable MWh rather than partnership headlines.
insights.quote: demand, corporate partnerships and policy support are not the same as projects delivering affordable electricity on time
insights.locator: Rising electricity demand, especially from AI

insights.claim: The central investable question for nuclear and geothermal is whether renewed momentum converts into repeatable deployment rather than one-off projects.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Track second- and third-of-a-kind projects as the real signal of scalability.
insights.quote: The central question is whether both technologies can turn renewed momentum into repeatable deployment.
insights.locator: Rising electricity demand, especially from AI

insights.claim: Nuclear uprates and restarts of existing reactors could add capacity sooner than new builds, while small modular reactors are more likely to arrive in the 2030s.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Near-term nuclear capacity upside accrues to existing-fleet owners; SMR developers face a long pre-revenue runway into the 2030s.
insights.quote: small modular reactors are more likely to arrive in the 2030s
insights.locator: Host Caitlin Connolly, Senior Analyst at Wood Mackenzie

insights.claim: Nuclear fuel recycling could improve fuel security and reduce the volume of material requiring disposal, but would not remove the need for a geologic repository (per Jenifer Shafer, Colorado School of Mines).
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Recycling is a partial waste/fuel-security lever, not a substitute for a repository; waste policy risk persists.
insights.quote: would not remove the need for a repository
insights.locator: Host Caitlin Connolly, Senior Analyst at Wood Mackenzie

insights.claim: Cost, safeguards and social license remain the central challenges for nuclear, and progress through the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission is a key signal to watch.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Use NRC licensing milestones as leading indicators for nuclear developer timelines and valuations.
insights.quote: progress through the Nuclear Regulatory Commission is a key signal to watch
insights.locator: Host Caitlin Connolly, Senior Analyst at Wood Mackenzie

insights.claim: Enhanced geothermal systems target heat in deep rock beyond the limited areas served by conventional hydrothermal resources; drilling and reservoir engineering have advanced, but the test now is sustaining heat flow economically over time.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: EGS risk has shifted from drilling feasibility to long-run reservoir economics; watch decline rates and O&M costs.
insights.locator: Enhanced geothermal systems aim to reach heat

insights.claim: Enhanced geothermal projects must manage water loss, scaling, corrosion and reservoir performance to be economic.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: These operational risks are the key diligence items for EGS developers and their offtakers.
insights.quote: managing water loss, scaling, corrosion and reservoir performance
insights.locator: Enhanced geothermal systems aim to reach heat

insights.claim: Geothermal power purchase agreements scheduled for delivery in 2028–2030 are an important test of delivery but not yet proof of scale (per Anna Littlefield, Payne Institute).
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: 2028–2030 contracted-delivery performance is the catalyst window for geothermal credibility.
insights.quote: an important test of delivery, not yet proof of scale
insights.locator: Enhanced geothermal systems aim to reach heat

insights.claim: Colorado's geothermal permitting and development efforts, including assessing whether treated oil and gas produced water can support geothermal circulation, may offer lessons for other states.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Produced-water reuse could link oil and gas operators to geothermal and ease EGS water constraints; watch Colorado as a template.
insights.locator: Enhanced geothermal systems aim to reach heat

insights.claim: Nuclear's binding constraints are fuel, waste and project execution, while geothermal's are durable reservoirs plus water and induced-seismicity concerns.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Different risk stacks mean different diligence: execution/waste for nuclear, subsurface/water for geothermal.

insights.claim: Both nuclear and geothermal depend on community trust, and developers need to listen to local concerns and share monitoring data rather than assume technical explanations alone will win support.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Social license is a schedule risk; developers with transparent monitoring may permit faster.
insights.quote: rather than assume technical explanations alone will win support

insights.claim: Over the next five years the clearest evidence for clean firm power will be projects reaching operation and performing as promised, alongside nuclear licensing progress and geothermal delivering contracted power reliably.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Set a five-year scorecard: CODs, NRC licenses, and geothermal PPA delivery.
